turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Right so, blood pressure is 118 over 74, and the pulse is 82. You're grand there.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that high? I'm all over the place, I hardly slept with the scratching.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're not high. Tell me about the scratching, in your own words.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's this itch between my fingers, and around my waist where the jeans sit. I can't stop at it.
[SEG0005] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And I'm at it too, and the small fella—
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): He's three. Sorry, I talk over people when I'm nervous. He wakes clawing at his tummy.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's alright. How long has the itch been going on for you?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. Well I blamed a new washing powder at first. It didn't ease though.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): And roughly how long?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): About three weeks. Maybe a bit more. It's desperate at night, I'm still going at two.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever with it, or feeling fluish in yourself?
[SEG0012] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She was eating away, grand in herself. My da is on metforman for his sugar, I thought maybe this was a sugar rash.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no fever. And I haven't diabetes. I'm not on any of that.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Grand. That metforman is his da's, not yours. Any allergy to creams or tablets?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I know of.
[SEG0016] person_1 (NURSE): I'll say, when my own little fella had a dose of this last winter I was up to my eyes in washing. Fierce altogether.

[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): The itchy rash between the fingers and at the waist, worse at night, and the people at home itching with you, I'd say this is scabies. The mite burrows into the very top of the skin, and the itch is your body reacting to it, not the creature biting you all night.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Scabies? Oh God. Are we dirty? I hoover every day. How did we get it?
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): It is nothing to do with being dirty. It passes by close skin contact, it's very ordinary, and it does not mean the house is filthy.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): And the burrowing, does that mean it's in my blood? I'm sorry, I just keep asking.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): It stays in the surface of the skin. It does not get into the blood. The finger webs and the waistband are simply where it likes to sit.
[SEG0022] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): My wrists have been itchy maybe a fortnight. Not a patch on hers.

[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back to you. Itchy rash between the fingers and round the waist for about three weeks, worse at night, no fever, no allergies, and your partner and the three year old are scratching as well. That is the scabies pattern.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): So what do we actually do? Do myself, my partner, and the small fella all need the cream? We're all in the one house. And do I ring the creche?
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. Permethrin five percent cream, for you, your partner, and the child, all on the same night. I'll take you through it step by step.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Is five percent not very strong? I saw a one percent bottle online, permetrin or something.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): That one percent is a different product, not for this. You want the five percent cream. Lyclear is the name you'll see on the box.
[SEG0028] person_1 (NURSE): I can show you the putting on of it after, if that settles the nerves.

[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have a shower first and let the skin cool and dry. Then the cream goes on every inch from the jawline down, between the fingers, under the nails, the waist, the belly button, the soles of the feet, and the genitals. Don't skip the skin under rings.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Not the face? What about him, he's only three, what about his face and hair?

[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): He's three, so he gets the same as the two of you, jawline down. We only do the scalp and the face in babies under two, or if the head is itchy. Keep it out of the eyes and the mouth.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No, the face is grand on me anyway. How long does it stay on before a wash?
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Eight to twelve hours. Overnight is the handy way, then wash it off in the morning. You do the very same again seven days later, even if the itch is easing.
[SEG0034] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And the duvet, she was half saying we should bin—
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't say bin it. I said I didn't know. I trail off when I panic.

[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Don't bin a thing. Hot wash the clothes, the towels and the bedclothes from the last three days, at sixty degrees. Anything that won't wash, seal it in a bag for three days. The mite dies quickly once it's off the skin.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Sixty. Right. What about the couch? And can I work tomorrow? I'm on the till in a cafe.

[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): No spray for the couch. Hoover it if you like, that's plenty. You can go to work the morning after the first treatment, once the cream is washed off. Ring the creche and let them know, and he can go back the day after he's treated.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): I've been taking a ceterizine, ten milligrams, in the morning, from the chemist, for the itch. Do I stop that?

[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep the cetirizine. It only dulls the itch, it does not kill the mite. The itch can hang on for two or three weeks after the cream has done its job, because the skin is still reacting.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Two or three weeks after? What if it's still as bad? I won't cope.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the itch is still as bad three weeks after the second treatment, come back and I'll look again. No blood tests today.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): And you're sure it's not eczema? My cousin had eczema something fierce. Sorry, more questions.

[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Your cousin's eczema is not yours. Looking at the skin, it's dry and scratched between the fingers, with a few tiny burrow marks, and there's a faint rash along the waistband. No weeping, and no sign of cellulitis.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, do we do two nights together or do we wait the week? I get muddled.

[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): One night now, and once more in seven days. Not two nights running. The prescription will be at reception, enough permethrin for the three of you, two applications each. You'll be grand.

Treat the three-year-old from the jawline down like the adults; scalp and face only for babies under two or if the head is itchy

Vacuum the couch if wanted; return to cafe work the morning after the first treatment; tell the creche and the child may return the day after treatment
Continue cetirizine each morning for the itch; the itch may persist for two to three weeks after treatment

spec.situation: Itchy rash between fingers and at the waist, worse at night, partner and child also itch; permethrin cream explained step by step; household treatment and washing advice.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

features: interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
